Activation steering works by adding a vector — typically extracted as the difference in mean activations between a concept-present and concept-absent distribution — directly to the residual stream at some layer, nudging the model's internal state toward a target concept during inference. The central question in compositionality is whether you can add multiple such vectors simultaneously and get behavior that reflects the conjunction of those concepts, or whether interference patterns, magnitude collapse, or feature suppression cause the result to be something alien to both. The key concepts to hold in mind are: linear representation hypothesis (concepts correspond to approximately linear directions in activation space), superposition (models pack more features than dimensions by using quasi-orthogonal directions), and the residual stream as a communication bus where each layer reads and writes additively. A beginner assumes that near-orthogonality of steering vectors means they compose cleanly — what an expert worries about is that while the directions may be orthogonal, the downstream circuits that read those directions are not independent: a single MLP neuron or attention head may be sensitive to multiple steered features simultaneously, creating nonlinear cross-talk that produces outputs no individual vector predicts. The expert also worries about norm: stacking vectors inflates the residual stream magnitude in ways that interact badly with layernorm, potentially causing the model to operate in an activation regime it never encountered during training, making the "concept" unrecognizable to later layers regardless of directional accuracy.

For semantically related but geometrically near-orthogonal vectors — think "anger" and "frustration" directions extracted from Llama-2-13B — circuit-level cross-talk is almost certainly the dominant failure mode, precisely because orthogonality eliminates the simpler explanation. The vectors won't cancel or reinforce each other in the stream, but downstream MLP layers trained on correlated semantic content will have weight matrices that effectively project both directions onto overlapping intermediate features; the circuits that process "anger" were shaped by training data where anger and frustration co-occur, so they respond to both steering inputs even when those inputs are geometrically separated. Distinguishing the two experimentally requires a double dissociation: first, measure the cosine similarity of the gradient of a target behavior with respect to each vector (directional interference shows up here as unexpected alignment), then ablate individual MLP neurons or attention heads at the layer immediately downstream of your injection point and check whether composed-vector outputs collapse differently than single-vector outputs — circuit cross-talk will localize to specific components, while directional interference is diffuse across all downstream computation. Turner et al.'s activation addition work (2023) on GPT-2 implicitly shows this: "banana" steering produces semantically coherent but globally weird outputs consistent with circuit disruption rather than clean vector addition. A clean control is to take two concepts with similar geometric separation but low semantic correlation (e.g., "anger" and "royalty") and compare behavioral degradation under composition — if the semantically related pair degrades more despite equal orthogonality, cross-talk is the mechanism.

The observable failure mode shifts from "wrong output" to "incoherent output" — the model produces text that's locally fluent but globally inconsistent, because some circuits see the steered concept while others see the unsteered input, and the two streams of computation produce contradictory signals that later layers can't reconcile. Contrast this with injecting at the correct write layer: failure there looks more like magnitude-induced distribution shift (the concept is present but too loud), whereas wrong-layer injection produces a distinctive signature of semantic inconsistency across a single generation. When you inject a composed steering vector, the modified residual stream gets projected through every subsequent attention layer's Q, K, and V weight matrices — meaning your steering perturbation directly shifts query and key vectors, potentially re-routing attention to entirely different token positions than the unsteered forward pass used. This can help compositionality in cases where the target concepts naturally co-attend to compatible context: if steering toward "formal register" and "French language" simultaneously causes attention heads to upweight positions containing formal French tokens already in context, the re-routing reinforces the composition. The hurt case is more common and more insidious: vectors extracted from different input distributions carry implicit assumptions about which tokens should be attended to, and when composed, their conflicting attention biases can cause heads to attend to positions that are neither semantically relevant to concept A nor concept B — a kind of attention averaging that destroys the structured information retrieval both concepts depend on. Anthropic's interpretation work on superposition and the findings from Hernandez et al. (2023) on linearity of factual associations both implicitly assume attention patterns remain stable under intervention, which is precisely the assumption that breaks here — the linearity holds in activation space but not in the dynamical system that produces those activations. A concrete diagnostic is to compare attention entropy before and after steering injection: clean single-vector steering typically sharpens or shifts attention patterns predictably, while composed vectors that hurt compositionality show attention entropy increasing — heads becoming more diffuse and uncertain — which you can measure directly by computing KL divergence between steered and unsteered attention distributions across layers and checking whether the divergence scales superlinearly with the number of composed vectors.

A model trained to expose stable steering subspaces would need an objective that simultaneously rewards behavioral response to injected concept vectors and penalizes attention pattern disruption — concretely, something like: for a batch of (prompt, concept vector) pairs, maximize the KL divergence between steered and unsteered output distributions (so steering actually works) while minimizing the KL divergence between steered and unsteered attention patterns across all heads (so routing is preserved), with the tension between these two terms forcing the model to carve out residual stream directions that influence MLP-mediated concept representation without touching attention's input subspace. β-VAE, the pathology is over-disentanglement: if the model learns to fully isolate steering subspaces from attention, it may do so by making those subspaces informationally shallow, storing concepts in directions that MLPs can read but that carry no structural information about token relationships, producing a model that's steerable but loses compositional generalization in normal inference. A second pathology is Goodhart's law applied to mechanistic structure: the model learns to keep attention patterns numerically stable under steering not by genuinely separating the subspaces but by developing compensatory attention heads that re-route after the injection layer to undo the perturbation, making the model appear steerable in shallow evaluations while actually suppressing the intervention internally — a mechanistic analogue of sycophancy. The training distribution also matters critically: if concept vectors used during training are drawn from a narrow distribution (e.g., only sentiment and topic vectors), the model learns stable subspaces only for those concept types, and novel steering vectors at deployment time fall outside the trained-stable region, potentially causing worse attention disruption than an untrained model because the architecture has been warped to accommodate a specific subspace geometry. Anthropic's work on representation engineering and the broader literature on activation addition suggest that current models already have partially stable steering subspaces by accident — the pathology of explicit training is that you'd be optimizing something that currently works approximately for free, risking the introduction of new failure modes in exchange for marginal gains in the regimes you tested.

Detecting compensatory suppression requires comparing the steering vector's causal footprint at the injection layer against its footprint at the final layer before the unembedding — specifically, you'd compute the projection of the residual stream onto the steering direction at each layer post-injection, and if that projection decays faster than expected from normal residual stream mixing, you have evidence of active suppression rather than passive dilution. The smoking gun is a layer where the projection drops sharply while attention outputs at that layer show anomalously high magnitude in the direction opposite to the steering vector — meaning a specific set of heads is writing a cancellation signal, which you can confirm by ablating those heads and checking whether the steering effect is restored, following the same attribution patching methodology used in the IOI circuit work (Wang et al., 2022). Behavioral evaluations are indeed systematically unreliable for exactly the reason this implies: a model can produce outputs indistinguishable from an unsteered forward pass while the concept vector is present in intermediate layers, suppressed only at the final readout, or conversely can produce outputs that look like the steered concept while the residual stream projection onto the target direction is minimal and the output is driven by superficial token correlations rather than genuine concept activation. This is the mechanistic analogue of a problem already known in probing literature — Ravichander et al. (2021) and subsequent work showed that a probe detecting a concept in activations doesn't imply that concept is used by the model's computation, and the same dissociation applies in reverse: behavioral expression of a concept doesn't imply the steering vector's direction is causally active in producing that expression. The implication for the field is uncomfortable: the standard evaluation pipeline of "inject vector, observe output, declare success" conflates three distinct things — presence of the concept direction in the stream, causal role of that direction in the output, and behavioral expression of the concept — and compensatory heads can decouple all three simultaneously, meaning rigorous steering evaluation requires activation analysis at multiple layers, not just behavioral scoring.

Causal scrubbing (Chan et al., 2022) is the right class of tool because it demands a hypothesis about which nodes and edges in the computational graph are responsible for a behavior and then tests that hypothesis by replacing activations with counterfactuals from a reference distribution — but applying it to a steered model breaks a foundational assumption: the reference distribution used for counterfactual replacement is drawn from natural forward passes, and a steered forward pass is by construction outside that distribution, meaning the scrubbing procedure's notion of "what this node would compute on an unrelated input" no longer provides a valid baseline for measuring causal contribution. Concretely, when you scrub a node in a steered model by replacing its activation with a sample from the natural distribution, you're not isolating that node's causal role — you're also removing the steering signal that was upstream of it, conflating "this node doesn't matter" with "this node was carrying the steered concept and we just deleted it," which produces false negatives in the hypothesis test. A second breakage point is that causal scrubbing requires specifying a correspondence between the hypothesis's abstract variables and concrete model components, but steering vectors often activate distributed representations with no clean node-level boundary — the "anger" concept might be partially expressed across 40 attention heads and 12 MLP layers simultaneously, making the required hypothesis specification intractable without a prior mechanistic decomposition that we typically don't have. The fix requires augmenting the reference distribution to include steered forward passes with varied steering vectors, so counterfactual replacement samples from a distribution that preserves the steered activation regime — essentially building a scrubbing framework that treats the steering vector as an additional input variable rather than a perturbation to a fixed computational graph. This reframing is non-trivial because it means the hypothesis being tested is no longer "does subgraph G compute behavior B" but "does subgraph G compute behavior B as a function of both input tokens and steering vector," which requires specifying how the hypothesis graph is supposed to use the steering signal, pushing the verification problem back to requiring mechanistic understanding as a prerequisite rather than a output.
